article.articleHeadline: DRC: Authorities urged to protect children amid Ebola outbreak - ACP
article.articleSummary: Kinshasa, June 10, 2026: An appeal to authorities, scientists and the community to protect children from Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) as the outbreak continues in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Solange Ghonda, Special Ambassador for Children, urged intensified research and mobilization to save lives and protect vulnerable children, describing Ebola as a disease occurring exclusively on the African continent. She called for mobilizing the international community and leveraging women as the primary communication relay for preventive measures, especially in remote villages, to encourage rapid adoption of life-saving practices. Better information, she said, enables the population to act to prevent new cases from becoming outbreaks. Combating Ebola requires solidarity, innovation and partnerships among academic institutions, governments and international organizations, with WHO declaring the outbreak a Public Health Emergency of International Concern.

article.articleHeadline: From Hantavirus to Ebola, pandemic preparedness must become broader
article.articleSummary: Two concurrent outbreaks defined the landscape as of 11 June 2026: Hantavirus infections aboard the MV Hondius in early April with 11 suspected cases and 3 deaths, and Ebola resurfacing in Central Africa with ongoing transmission. Ebola benefited from decades of surveillance and rapid detection; Hantavirus exposed gaps in early recognition, especially on cruise ships and in unusual settings. Ebola's clinical-response capacity was mature; Hantavirus revealed weaker front-end recognition. Risk communication favored Ebola, though uncertainty and misinformation persisted. Funding since 2024-25 has declined, with US aid cuts and weaker global institutions, underscoring the need for systemic, broad-based preparedness spanning surveillance, science, healthcare and governance. Written by a virologist and chair of Ignite Life Science Foundation (India), the piece calls for sustained, cross-border preparedness for unusual pathogens and travel-related risks.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola outbreak: What you need to know | Project HOPE
article.articleSummary: Ebola outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda continue to pose major public-health risks. Front-line health workers face high exposure as PPE and IPC supplies remain limited, complicating safe delivery of basic health services. Ongoing border restrictions exist between DRC and Uganda, with unofficial crossings continuing; humanitarian corridors are prioritized. Community resistance to recognizing and responding to Ebola hampers containment efforts, potentially fueling transmission and burnout among caregivers and families. Ebola, caused by a Filoviridae virus, is most prevalent in Central and East Africa, with fruit bats as the natural reservoir; outbreaks start when humans contact infected wild animals or contaminated materials. The virus spreads through direct contact with blood, body fluids, tissues, or contaminated objects. Early detection, isolation, vaccination where available, and supportive care are key to control.

In March 2026, he developed eye-area vesicles, photophobia, and tearing, diagnosed as ophthalmic shingles; after partial recovery, he then contracted herpangina with fever and pharyngitis, followed by vestibular neuritis due to herpes simplex virus invading the inner-ear vestibular nerve, with vertigo and gait instability. Physicians attribute the rapid, sequential infections to immune decline from aging and long-term sleep deprivation amid a company transformation. They note varicella-zoster virus lies dormant in most people and can reactivate when immunity wanes. The doctor advises shingles vaccination for those over 40 to reduce incidence and lingering nerve pain. Report from the ENT department of Fujian University of Traditional Chinese Medicine Affiliated Third People’s Hospital.

article.articleHeadline: Confirmed Ebola virus cases near 600 as outbreak in Democratic Republic of Congo grows
article.articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo nears 600 confirmed cases with at least 100 deaths, escalating over two weeks by more than eightfold and affecting 25 health zones. Most cases are in Ituri and North Kivu, with some in neighboring Uganda. The circulating strain is Bundibugyo, for which testing kits (designed for Zaire Ebola) may miss detections, and there is no vaccine or treatment specific to Bundibugyo. Contact tracing stands at 64% (vs the usual 80–90%), impeding containment amid security concerns from armed groups and ongoing diagnosis delays. WHO’s June 9 rapid risk assessment warns of considerable outbreak expansion, increased mobility, and patients avoiding treatment facilities, with community mistrust hindering detection, tracing, and isolation. Ituri’s health infrastructure shows critical gaps (prevention/control scores below 30%). An imported/exported case trace: a Congolese national traveled to the UAE via Uganda, later returning to Uganda; UAE authorities found no secondary cases.

article.articleSummary: As of 2026-06-11, malaria elimination in Asia-Pacific remains precarious: keeping zero cases is harder than attaining it, requiring sustained political will, robust surveillance, and ongoing funding through the final elimination phase. In the Greater Mekong Subregion, Cambodia has eliminated indigenous transmission and now aims to prevent re-establishment amid cross-border movement and migrant workers. China was malaria-free in 2021; Timor-Leste achieved certification last year; Sri Lanka is malaria-free, and Bhutan is expected to join. Certification does not end risk; countries must maintain rapid detection of imported cases and run regular simulations to test outbreak responses. Global Fund financing for 18 APAC elimination countries is projected to fall about 40% in the next cycle, prompting greater reliance on domestic resources and strengthened cross-border coordination to reach the 2030 elimination target.

article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Summer sees a high incidence of gastrointestinal infectious diseases; remember basic food hygiene practices.
article.articleSummary: Summer heat and humidity in China raise the incidence of gastrointestinal infectious diseases, including bacterial dysentery (shigellosis), norovirus infection, and food poisoning, spread mainly by the fecal-oral route. Prevention hinges on basic food hygiene: choose fresh, safe ingredients; avoid expired or unknown-source foods; do not collect wild mushrooms or plants. Separate raw and cooked foods during preparation; use different utensils; cook meat, eggs, and seafood thoroughly. When eating out, pick hygienic, licensed establishments and avoid street vendors and raw or cold foods. Maintain personal hygiene: wash hands with soap under running water for at least 20 seconds before meals and after bathroom use, after handling raw food, or touching public items. Refrigerate leftovers within 24 hours and reheat thoroughly before reuse. Drink boiled or bottled water. If symptoms such as nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, or diarrhea appear, seek medical care promptly.

article.articleHeadlineTranslated: The mosquito 'invader' that threatens Europe — What do experts fear?
article.articleSummary: As of June 11, 2026, Japanese encephalitis virus (JEV) risk in Europe centers on Culex tritaeniorhynchus, a mosquito species whose updated ECDC maps show potential spread to Southern Europe, including Greece; no European cases have been recorded. JEV is endemic mainly in East and Southeast Asia, with roughly half the world’s population in endemic areas (~3 billion people). Transmission involves mosquitoes feeding on wild birds (primarily herons) and pigs as amplifying hosts; humans are dead-end hosts. Introduction to Greece would require an infected mosquito or an infected heron; local wetlands limit such events. Most infections are asymptomatic or mild; about 1 in 250 develop neuroinvasive encephalitis, presenting high fever, neck stiffness, and photophobia. Mortality among encephalitis cases is ~15–20%, and about 40% of survivors have lasting neurological sequelae. A vaccine exists for travelers to endemic regions.

article.articleSummary: Coprological analysis of Callithrix jacchus in Northeastern Brazil detected Primasubulura jacchi eggs (66–75 μm × 55–65 μm; thick, smooth shell), morphologically compatible with P. jacchi, indicating high intestinal parasitism. The finding underscores One Health interfaces among wildlife, domestic animals, and humans in northeastern Brazil and highlights the need for regional surveys.

article.articleHeadlineTranslated: "Even last-resort antibiotics are useless" Emergency... The identity of the antibiotic-resistant bacteria that have reached eight-month-old infants.
article.articleSummary: Six infants aged 8–12 months hospitalized for acute diarrhea in southern China were found to carry highly carbapenem-resistant Salmonella enterica, despite no prior hospitalization, antibiotic exposure, or travel to high-risk areas. The strains showed broad resistance to penicillins and cephalosporins and reduced susceptibility or resistance to carbapenems, the last-resort antibiotics. Genomic analysis revealed clonal signals in some isolates, suggesting possible transmission within healthcare settings and potentially the broader community, while other isolates showed divergence, indicating ongoing local spread in the region. The presence of carbapenemase genes and related resistance determinants in gut bacteria points to horizontal gene transfer. Current hospital diagnostic tests may miss some carbapenemase producers, risking inappropriate antibiotic therapy and treatment delays that could be fatal in infants. Researchers call for more precise, multi-target diagnostics and enhanced surveillance to assess community spread in southern China. Published in Journal of Infection, 2026 issue.

Prevention emphasizes boiled water, fully cooked foods, and reporting exposures; contaminated lettuce and shellfish are highlighted risks.

article.articleSummary: Nipah virus case reported in Kerala's Kozhikode district: a 43-year-old man from Feroke tested positive and is on ventilator support. Samples have been sent to the National Institute of Virology (NIV), Pune, for confirmation, with final results expected soon. He was admitted to a private hospital and later moved to Government Medical College, Kozhikode, where he remains critical. Contact tracing and quarantine measures are in place as authorities investigate the infection source, with the minister noting the man had recently rented and cleaned a godown. Nipah is a zoonotic virus carried by fruit bats and can infect pigs and humans; initial symptoms include fever, headache, muscle pain and respiratory problems, and progression can cause encephalitis, seizures and coma. Kerala has seen multiple Nipah outbreaks since 2018; prevention emphasizes avoiding contact with sick pigs/bats and avoiding contaminated raw date palm sap, plus standard hospital infection control. A review meeting is planned.

article.articleHeadline: Why India's deadly dengue crisis is now no longer confined to the monsoons
article.articleSummary: Dengue in India is no longer confined to the monsoon. By February 2026, NCVBDC reported 6,927 dengue cases, with Tamil Nadu highest at 2,873, followed by Maharashtra 786, Kerala 670, and Karnataka 560, indicating earlier and more persistent transmission. A Gurugram case (Nitin Sharma) illustrates pre-monsoon illness; dengue is mosquito-borne, with symptoms such as high fever, headaches, severe body aches and fatigue. Transmission previously peaked post-monsoon, but rising temperatures, erratic rainfall and urbanisation are expanding the transmission window. Studies note that long-term exposure to fine particulate air pollution is linked to higher dengue mortality, underscoring climate and pollution roles in severity. National totals show 289,235 infections and 485 deaths in 2023; 233,519 and 297 in 2024; 121,824 and 131 in 2025. Health authorities urge year-round surveillance and earlier warning systems to counter the year-round threat.

article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Hantavirus: A Silent Threat Hidden in Rodent Homes
article.articleSummary: Hantavirus causes about 200,000 global infections annually, with 90% of cases in China. Iranian antibody surveys show silent circulation of the virus, though no clinically confirmed cases have been identified yet. A hantavirus-focused infectious diseases seminar at Labbafinejad Hospital in Tehran, funded by Pfizer and Standard Co, emphasized healthcare preparedness; Iran currently has no reported cases, though studies in Isfahan suggest possible presence. Hantavirus presents in two main forms: hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and a respiratory syndrome. Virus types include Hantaan, Amur, and European/northern-Russian strains, with Sin Nombre prominent in the Americas. Seroprevalence ranges: Paraguay 40%, Argentina 17%, Panama 13%, northern Sweden ~20%, and central Iran about 4.5%. Transmission is via inhalation of rodent excreta; urban rodent-associated strains exist, with rural types more common elsewhere. Climate change may raise rodent populations and spread; Turkey has reported cases, and some western U.S. states are affected.

article.articleHeadlineTranslated: In the summer when mosquitoes are on the rise, be especially careful of "this virus."
article.articleSummary: Zika virus poses renewed risk as summer mosquito activity rises, especially for pregnant travelers. Transmitted mainly by Aedes aegypti, infection during pregnancy can cause fetal microcephaly and other congenital abnormalities. Many infections are mild or asymptomatic; when symptoms occur, they include fever, rash, joint pain, conjunctivitis, myalgia, and headache, lasting a few days to about a week. The CDC estimates about one in seven babies born to infected pregnant women may have health issues. Zika also spreads via sexual contact, blood transfusion, and shared needles; there are no approved vaccines or treatments, making prevention crucial. Zika was first identified in 1947 in Uganda’s Zika Forest, triggered a large 2015 Brazil outbreak, and WHO declared a PHEIC in 2016. CNN advises long sleeves and repellents, with heightened caution for pregnancy-related travelers to affected regions.

article.articleHeadline: Democratic Republic of Congo's Ebola testing has improved, but it's still not enoughExBulletin
article.articleSummary: Testing capacity for Ebola in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo has improved to seven labs able to process Bundibugyo samples, using new machines like RADI-One, with some sites handling up to 100 tests per day on-site, reducing dependence on Kinshasa. The outbreak's early spread was driven by a mis-diagnosis when Bunia's lab used Bundibugyo-compatible equipment that couldn't detect the circulating strain, delaying confirmation. While backlogs have mostly cleared, officials warn the system remains behind as transmission rises and case loads grow. Sample transport remains a bottleneck: days to reach a lab, and some areas inaccessible due to conflict and poor roads. No rapid tests are approved for Bundibugyo yet; rapid tests exist for other Ebola strains and could enable on-site isolation and contact tracing, but development may take weeks to months.

article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Containing the Ebola outbreak, a difficult task hampered by misinformation.
article.articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (Ituri region, Bunia) is being hampered by misinformation that delays care and endangers staff. About 100 Ebola deaths have occurred in the DRC; in Ituri, roughly one in three people doubt Ebola exists. Rumors range from disease denial to accusations against health authorities and promotion of unvalidated treatments, spreading via social media and village discussions. WHO and health experts warn misinformation can undermine surveillance, contact tracing, and safe burial practices, destabilizing the outbreak response. Experts advocate trusted community engagement, using ambassadors in local languages and collaboration with traditional leaders, recovered patients, and healers to restore confidence and strengthen control efforts.

They recommend consulting a doctor to plan RSV prevention during the rainy season.

article.articleHeadline: Wagub Gorontalo Ajak Generasi Muda Aktif Cegah Penularan HIV-AIDS
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Gorontalo Vice Governor Urges the Youth to Actively Prevent HIV/AIDS Transmission.
article.articleSummary: HIV/AIDS prevention drive in Gorontalo Province, Indonesia, led by the Vice Governor, mobilizes youths to curb transmission. Emphasizing comprehensive reproductive health literacy and reducing stigma, the plan outfits Gen Z and Millennials as peer educators to promote early detection and educate their communities, including People living with HIV/AIDS (PLHIV). The ABCDE framework—Abstinence, Be Faithful, Condom use, Drug abstinence, and Education—guides individual prevention and counters misinformation. Government and Health Department collaboration with civil society provides adolescent-friendly counseling and easier access to health screenings across Gorontalo. Emphasis on healthy living and environmental hygiene as a foundation for resilience. Officials pursue the Three Zero vision: zero new infections, zero AIDS-related deaths, and zero stigma. article.articleSummary: Kisumu County, Kenya, is on high alert for an Ebola threat amid ongoing outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Uganda. No case has been detected yet, but the county, a major transport hub along routes linking Kenya with DRC, Uganda and the Great Lakes region, faces a very high risk of imported infection. Surveillance is activated at health facilities and entry points, including Kisumu International Airport, bus parks, and Lake Victoria beaches, with symptomatic screening and temperature checks. At least five suspected Ebola cases have been tested since regional outbreaks began; all results were negative. Preparedness includes county rapid response teams, training on case identification, specimen collection, and isolation, plus isolation units in Level Four hospitals and PPE stock mobilization. Samples are transported to KEMRI labs for rapid testing; coordination with NPHI, MoH, and WHO is ongoing.

article.articleHeadline: Kerala on alert after Nipah case detected in Kozhikode
article.articleSummary: Nipah virus detected in Kozhikode, Kerala, after a 43-year-old man from Farook tested positive, triggering emergency containment measures. The patient, who had been carrying out cleaning work at a structure with heavy bat presence, developed Nipah-like symptoms and was moved to an isolation ward at Kozhikode Medical College Hospital. Initial laboratory tests at the Medical College laboratory confirmed Nipah infection, and samples have been sent to the National Institute of Virology (NIV), Pune, for final confirmation. Authorities have launched containment and contact-tracing measures; the case marks a fresh Nipah alert in the region. The report underscores bat-to-human spillover as the suspected transmission route, with authorities monitoring close contacts and exposure risk in the Kozhikode district. As of 2026-06-11, the patient remains in isolation awaiting NIV confirmation.

article.articleSummary: As of 11 June 2026, the United States is providing an additional $20 million (about Sh2.59 billion) to strengthen Ebola preparedness in Kenya, Burundi, Rwanda and South Sudan, bringing State Department funding for Ebola response and preparedness to more than $220 million. article.articleHeadline: Állattartási szokások magyarázzák a Kolumbusz utáni amerikai járványokat
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Animal husbandry practices explain the post-Columbian epidemics in the Americas.
article.articleSummary: An analysis links post-Columbian Americas epidemics to long Eurasian animal husbandry, where dense cohabitation with cattle, pigs, sheep and poultry bred zoonotic pathogens that jump to humans (smallpox, measles, influenza, typhus, and whooping cough). In contrast, Andean and Mesoamerican regions had fewer domesticated species—llama, alpaca, turkey, and guinea pig—and lacked intense, ongoing close contact with such pathogens, leaving Indigenous populations immunologically naïve to introduced infections. During the Columbian Exchange, European diseases spread ahead of or with conquerors, with smallpox appearing around 1518 and contributing to demographic and societal collapse among the Inca and Aztec states. The disease flow was largely one-way, aside from debate over syphilis’ origin, with some associating late 15th-century European appearance to contact with the Americas and others proposing earlier Old World variants. Overall, Eurasian agrarian systems served as a vast evolutionary laboratory reshaping world history.

article.articleHeadline: Cứu sống bệnh nhân ho ra máu do di chứng lao phổi
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Life saved for patient with hemoptysis due to sequelae of pulmonary tuberculosis.
article.articleSummary: Left upper lobe lobectomy at Hoan My Can Tho Hospital in Can Tho, Vietnam, treated life-threatening hemoptysis due to sequelae of pulmonary tuberculosis. The patient, 67-year-old N.T.T. from Long Xuyen, An Giang Province, presented in emergency with moderate blood loss and a history of TB. CT showed collapse of the left upper lobe, old TB sequelae, and a large clot in the bronchus. A difficult 4-hour operation removed the diseased left upper lobe. After 7 days, the patient was stable and discharged. Hemoptysis is particularly dangerous in patients with prior TB or bronchiectasis. While bronchial artery embolization can control acute bleeding, surgical lobectomy provides definitive cure by removing the lesion and preventing recurrence.

article.articleHeadline: 新研究揭示蝙蝠冠状病毒跨物种传播屏障 -- 新闻 -- 科学网
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: New Study Reveals the Cross-Species Transmission Barrier of Bat Coronaviruses.
article.articleSummary: Rc-o319, a sarbecovirus isolated from the Japanese horseshoe bat (Rhinolophus cornutus), features a RBM with nine amino acid deletions, forming a distinctive beta-loop that mediates specific recognition of bat ACE2. Cryo-EM reveals that interactions with Rhinolophus cornutus ACE2 are enhanced by Asn38 glycosylation on the host receptor, which also dampens receptor usage by Rc-o319 and other sarbecoviruses. To gain mid-to-high affinity for human ACE2 would require coordinated changes in both the beta-loop and the RBM-loop; single-region changes are insufficient, indicating a substantial cross-species transmission barrier. ACE2 Asn38 glycosylation may represent a general host defense limiting sarbecovirus receptor engagement. The findings, underpinning structural bases of host adaptation, inform spillover risk assessments and were published in PLOS Pathogens, supported by national science programs in China.

article.articleHeadline: Dengue, Hepatitis - und Durchfall: So schützen sich Reisende vor Krankheiten
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Dengue, Hepatitis, and Diarrhea: How Travelers Protect Themselves from Illnesses.
article.articleSummary: Travel health guidance (2026) centers on dengue, hepatitis A, and traveler's diarrhea as persistent risks for both European and international trips. Core advice: pack a travel-health kit with anti-diarrheals, sunscreen, and effective insect protection; ensure routine vaccines (tetanus, measles, polio) are up to date; hepatitis A vaccination is broadly recommended where food/water safety varies. Vaccination decisions are itinerary-dependent: rabies vaccination may be prudent for trips to Bali or other areas with frequent animal contact; even hotel stays do not fully shield against foodborne illnesses or mosquito-borne diseases. Regional risk highlights include Southeast Asia (Thailand, Bali, Sri Lanka) with dengue; Africa (Kenya, Tanzania, Zanzibar) with malaria; the Caribbean (Dominican Republic, Hispaniola with Haiti) with dengue, chikungunya, diphtheria, meningococcal disease, and leptospirosis; South America (Brazil, Argentina, Peru) with yellow fever, extending toward Central America (Panama Canal region). Tailor vaccines and precautions to the destination and travel style.

article.articleSummary: Nipah virus case detected in Kerala, India, after a preliminary test on a 43-year-old man in Kozhikode; patient is critical and on ventilator at Government Medical College, with hospital staff quarantined. The man, a smalltime businessman, had rented and cleaned a godown, with possible exposure to fruit bats, the natural Nipah host per WHO. Transmission can occur from direct contact with infected animals (bats, possibly horses), consumption of contaminated fruits or raw date palm juice, and person-to-person spread, especially in overcrowded, poorly ventilated healthcare settings. Kerala’s Nipah history includes the first outbreak in Kozhikode in 2018 (17 of 18 infected died) and a total state death toll of 24 to date, with outbreaks often during monsoon. Globally, Nipah emerged in Malaysia (1998) and Singapore (1999); India/Bangladesh outbreaks in 2001; West Bengal (2007) with five deaths; Philippines (2014). No vaccine or cure exists.

article.articleHeadline: Vietnam reports over 50,000 dengue cases in 5 months as outbreak patterns shift
article.articleSummary: Vietnam reports over 50,000 dengue cases in five months, underscoring shifting outbreak patterns ahead of ASEAN Dengue Day in Hanoi. Infections stayed elevated into late 2025 rather than declining, and outbreaks are now across most regions, including northern provinces. Climate change, rapid urbanization, and unpredictable trends are driving transmission; the DENV-2 serotype is dominant, increasing severe-illness risk. The age distribution has shifted: children under 15 no longer predominate in southern Vietnam, with infections among children and adults now nearly equal. Severe complications can occur on days 3–5 of illness when fever subsides, and delayed treatment raises risk of shock, bleeding, organ failure, and death. article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Dr. Alangkorn warns of a rabies outbreak; several deaths have occurred, noting the infection is dangerous and carries a risk of death within 7–10 days.
article.articleSummary: Rabies outbreak warning in Thailand by Dr. Alangkorn Maharnon (TSPCA). Rabies virus infections have caused multiple deaths; the disease is deadly, with most victims dying within 7–10 days, though some cases take longer. Transmission comes from infected mammals; dogs and cats are common sources; there is no cure. Two forms: furious rabies (about 90%) with stiff neck, drooling, dilated eyes, aggression; paralytic rabies (about 10%) with hiding in dark places and weakness. Elephants can also be infected—usually via bites from stray dogs—with onset around 25 days; symptoms include neck stiffness, protruding eyes, stumbling, and death. Public guidance: vaccinate pets annually, keep them indoors, avoid contact with strays; if bitten, wash wounds with soap and water, apply antiseptic, and seek medical care promptly; do not slap or squeeze wounds. For bitten elephants, notify a veterinarian; past elephant cases have sometimes required four vaccine doses (16x the normal dose).

article.articleSummary: Shigella outbreak in Kerala, India, with 20 people infected and one child dead. Government has raised high alert; restaurants and hotels are being closed due to unsanitary conditions. Shigellosis, caused by Shigella, attacks the intestines, causing diarrhoea, abdominal cramps, fever, vomiting and weakness; severe cases may have blood in stool. Transmission is mainly through contaminated food and water, with poor hygiene in food handling facilitating spread. Health authorities have increased surveillance across districts and launched checks in schools and other sensitive areas; some student cases reported, though most patients are stable. No laboratory confirmation details are provided. Officials say the situation is under control but urge vigilance. If after eating out you have severe diarrhoea, fever or abdominal pain, seek medical care rather than dismissing it as routine food poisoning. Ongoing outbreak monitoring as of 11 June 2026 in Kerala.

article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Research Seeks New Treatment for Schistosomiasis | Fiocruz Portal
article.articleSummary: Schistosomiasis caused by Schistosoma mansoni is the focus of a Fiocruz-led study reported in ACS Infectious Diseases, aiming to develop new drugs active against the parasite. In Brazil, about 1.5 million people live in transmission areas, with roughly 700 million at risk worldwide per the WHO. Praziquantel, in use for ~40 years, remains effective but has drawbacks—large tablets, bitter taste, and administration challenges for children; laboratory observations suggest possible resistance, though not yet seen in the field. The research, led by the IOC/Fiocruz and conducted with the University of Wisconsin–Madison, Aberystwyth University, and UFRJ, used laboratory assays and computational analyses to test eight praziquantel-analogs. Three compounds showed activity against adult worms, schistosomules, and larvae by binding to the parasite’s TRPM receptor; the receptor’s plasticity may guide future drug design. In vivo rodent infection models are planned to evaluate pharmacology and optimization potential.

Experts caution that vaccination must complement, not replace, vector control, sanitation, and surveillance. Sharma now uses repellents and daily checks for standing water.

article.articleHeadline: Study reveals 45 new toxins produced by bacteria associated with foodborne infections
article.articleSummary: As of 11 June 2026, researchers at the University of São Paulo's B3 RIDC analyzed 6,165 Salmonella enterica genomes across 149 serovars, identifying 128 toxin types, 45 of which are novel. Using the type VI secretion system, these effectors drive microbial competition, with some toxins also affecting eukaryotic cells, including fungi, algae, and mammals. While some toxins may contribute to human infections, confirmation requires linking specific strains to eukaryotic-targeting genes and experimental studies. Toxin repertoires vary by Salmonella subgroup; natural-environment isolates carry more effectors than patient-derived strains, suggesting environmental pressures foster diversification via recombination and natural selection. The findings illuminate bacterial competition strategies and could spur antibiotic development and biotechnological applications, with potential origins of some eukaryotic proteins in bacterial toxins. Study from USP/B3 RIDC, published in PLOS Biology and supported by FAPESP.

article.articleHeadline: WHO: Ebola risk remains low ahead of the Football World Cup
article.articleSummary: WHO says Ebola risk remains low ahead of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, urging fans to proceed with travel plans and enjoy the tournament despite outbreaks in parts of Africa. WHO Regional Director for Europe, Dr. Hans Henri P. Kluge, notes health assessments do not justify widespread travel restrictions and stresses following official guidance. Most reported cases are concentrated in remote areas of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, with Ebola transmission requiring direct contact with infected individuals, and screening measures for travelers from affected regions further reducing the risk of wider spread. WHO estimates about 80% of infections are asymptomatic; when present, symptoms include fever, headache, body aches, weakness, vomiting or nausea, skin rash or allergy-like symptoms, and swollen lymph nodes, typically within a few days to two weeks of the bite. article.articleSummary: As of 11 June 2026, in Keta Municipality, Volta Region, Ghana, health authorities urge the public to prevent malaria by consistent use of insecticide-treated nets and hygiene. article.articleSummary: Nipah virus case confirmed in Kerala: a 43-year-old man undergoing treatment in an isolation ward at Kozhikode Medical College Hospital; NIV Pune confirmed infection. Health authorities have intensified monitoring and contact tracing. Nipah is a zoonotic disease carried by fruit bats and can spread via contaminated foods (e.g., raw date palm juice) and through close contact between infected people; animals including pigs, dogs, cats, sheep and horses can also be infected. Prevention focuses on prompt symptom reporting, 14-day exposure monitoring, isolation, infection-control measures, and timely medical care; there is no specific antiviral treatment.

article.articleHeadline: Νέα ανακάλυψη: 45 τοξίνες από βακτήρια Salmonella " OnCamera.gr
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: New discovery: 45 toxins from Salmonella bacteria
article.articleSummary: Researchers from the University of São Paulo (USP) in Brazil identified 45 new toxins produced by Salmonella enterica, with some linked to foodborne infections. In a study conducted at the Center for Research on Bacteria and Bacteriophages Biology (B3 RIDC), they analyzed genetic data and the Type VI Secretion System (T6SS) that enables Salmonella to inject toxins into the environment or rival microbes. Using computational tools, they examined 6,165 samples from 149 Salmonella enterica serotypes, uncovering 128 toxin types, of which 45 are distinct from any known toxin. The findings show each Salmonella group has a unique toxin repertoire deployed via T6SS, likely shaped by environmental pressures and microbial competition. Implications include guiding the development of novel antibiotics and advancing understanding of human pathologies and biotechnology. Led by Robson Francisco de Souza, the work highlights potential future clinical and biotechnological applications.

article.articleHeadline: Contact Tracing Is The Biggest Weakness In Ebola Outbreak - Health Policy Watch
article.articleSummary: Ituri province, Democratic Republic of Congo, is the epicentre of the Ebola outbreak. By 9 June, 635 confirmed cases were reported, with 600 in Ituri. About 4,955 contacts have been recorded, but fewer than 60% traced, leaving roughly 12% of case contacts known and tested; each patient in Ituri's high-density mining towns could contact around 40 people, suggesting up to 24,000 potential contacts. Obstacles include rapid expansion, delayed detection, mobility, insecurity, and community resistance; attacks on health workers in Beni underline risks. Uganda reports 91% contact follow-up for 19 cases and no community transmission. Resource gaps: 540 staff needed, 84 available, and 98 ambulances, seven available. This is the third-largest Ebola outbreak in 20, with 27 health zones affected. 62% of cases are ages 15–44, and CFR among under-4s is 44%. Early-stage symptoms can resemble malaria, underscoring the need for better triage. Health workers account for 34 infections, five deaths.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola testing has improved in DRC, but still isn't nearly enough
article.articleSummary: Outbreak of Ebola Bundibugyo in northeastern Democratic Republic of Congo prompts testing challenges. Initial samples collected April 30 in Bunia tested negative on GeneXpert; later samples sent to Kinshasa yielded Ebola-positive results. Mid-May, authorities declared an Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak after a worrying delay, with suspected cases exceeding 1,100, risking rapid spread. Diagnostic capacity has since improved, with seven laboratories and a mobile lab able to process samples; Bunia can handle >100 per day, turnaround 1–12 hours. New deployment of the RADI-One device enables detection of Bundibugyo in smaller clinics, including Mongbwalu; Africa CDC aims for 50 RADI-One machines by end-June, in collaboration with WHO and KH Medical. Bottlenecks remain: sample transport across inaccessible areas amid conflict and displacement, plus community mistrust. Rapid tests could help speed isolation and even screen corpses to adjust burial practices, though they are less sensitive than lab tests.

article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Outbreaks of Shigella and Nipah in Kerala; cases detected in several districts have raised concerns.
article.articleSummary: Shigella outbreaks have been detected in Kerala across four districts: Wayanad (9 cases), Thiruvananthapuram (6), Kollam (2), and Kozhikode (3), with the health minister deeming the situation under control. Nipah infection is confirmed in a Ramanattukkara resident of Kozhikode district by NIV Pune; the patient is on ventilator at Kozhikode Medical College Hospital. A total of 77 contacts have been identified and isolated (58 health workers, 14 family members, 5 friends/colleagues); none of them are symptomatic so far. Shigella-related symptoms are reported in 578 people; 55 patients are hospitalised, 47 of them in Wayanad, where most cases involve school students. article.articleSummary: Nipah virus resurfaces in Kerala with a 43-year-old Feroke, Kozhikode district businessman testing positive. A preliminary PCR at Kozhikode Government Medical College Hospital indicated infection, and samples were confirmed positive by the National Institute for Virology, Pune. The patient, currently on ventilator support, experienced fever and encephalitis symptoms and is linked to exposure after cleaning a godown that may have bat droppings. A 72-person contact list has been drawn up (58 health workers, 14 family members); two are highest risk, 13 high-risk, the rest low risk. High-risk contacts are quarantined; rapid response teams are stock-taking PPE, gloves, masks, and medicines for quarantine. Nipah is a zoonotic virus carried by fruit bats. Since 2018 Kerala has reported 32 cases and 23 deaths; 2018 had 19 cases/17 deaths, with subsequent years showing fewer cases (2019: 1/0; 2021: 1/1; 2023: 6/2; 2024: 2/2; 2025: 2/1).

RSV-linked SARI increases in children ≤4; rhinovirus predominates in 5–14; influenza A rises among youth and older adults; influenza B increases in 5–14 and 15–49.

article.articleHeadlineTranslated: No vaccines or treatment and in a conflict zone: the Ebola outbreak is 'very concerning'.
article.articleSummary: Ebola outbreak in Ituri, northeast Democratic Republic of Congo, driven by the Bundibugyo variant, a strain with no vaccines or approved treatment. Three treatment centers have been opened; the response prioritizes isolation and safe burials to cut transmission. The World Health Organization notes a case fatality around 20-50%. Contact tracing for 21 days is essential, complicated by government- and rebel-controlled zones and cross-border coordination. More than 100,000 people were displaced in Ituri in early 2026, underscoring the need to bolster health systems for Ebola and other diseases such as cholera.

article.articleHeadline: Fresh Nipah virus case reported in Kerala
article.articleSummary: Fresh Nipah virus case reported in Kerala: National Institute of Virology, Pune, confirmed infection in a 43-year-old man at Kozhikode Medical College Hospital. The patient is in a specially prepared isolation ward and remains critical on ventilator support as contact tracing continues. Nipah is a zoonotic virus primarily carried by fruit bats; humans typically become infected via contaminated food products, especially raw date palm juice that may contain bat urine or saliva. This marks another active Nipah case in Kerala, underscoring ongoing surveillance and public health measures in the region.

Chikungunya has 12 notifications (10 discarded, 2 under analysis). The Municipal Health Department maintains environmental surveillance and vector-control actions: at-home visits to eliminate breeding sites, entomological monitoring with traps, case investigation and containment, intersectoral cleanup drives in priority areas, and enforcement of recurring-property inspections with compulsory cleaning of critical or abandoned sites. Nino Ribas says the urban presence of Aedes aegypti persists, so these measures continue during cooler periods to lower vector infestation and future transmission. Vaccination: the dengue vaccine Qdenga is available in two doses for 10–14-year-olds at Basic Health Units; the Butantan vaccine for health workers is temporarily suspended and does not affect Qdenga. Public can call Disque Dengue 0800-400-1893 or report online via Sisvas Londrina.

article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Beijing CDC: The seemingly clear and sweet “mountain spring water” is highly susceptible to contamination.
article.articleSummary: Beijing CDC cautions that seemingly clear and sweet mountain spring water in open environments is highly susceptible to contamination. In Beijing, such water can harbor pathogenic microorganisms—Escherichia coli, Salmonella, Cryptosporidium, and Giardia—and sources include wild animal feces and decaying vegetation, causing abdominal pain, diarrhea, acute gastroenteritis, and parasitic infections. Natural aquifers also leach heavy metals—lead, arsenic, cadmium, fluoride—while nearby pesticides, mining runoff, waste, and industrial discharges exacerbate risks; boiling cannot remove heavy metals or chemical pollutants, and long-term exposure may damage liver and kidneys or raise cancer risk. Seasonal algae growth and algal toxins may form in summer and are not fully destroyed by boiling. Water quality varies with season, so today’s safety does not guarantee tomorrow’s. Caution is advised when collecting or drinking mountain spring water in and around Beijing.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola testing has improved in DRC, but still isn't nearly enough
article.articleSummary: EBOLA Bundibugyo outbreak declared in northeastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), with initial samples in Bunia on April 30. GeneXpert testing was negative at first; later samples sent to Kinshasa for confirmation turned positive, prompting a mid-May outbreak declaration. Suspected cases exceed 1,100, with the CDC projecting up to 20,000 cases by August. Diagnostics were hampered by organism rarity not detected by GeneXpert, but capacity has improved: seven labs plus one mobile lab across northeastern DRC, with Bunia and Kinshasa processing over 100 samples per day and turnaround of 1–12 hours. Africa CDC aims for 50 RADI-One tests by end of June, enabling closer testing to sites like Mongbwalu; however, shortages of machines persist. Bottlenecks include sample transport, ongoing conflict, displacement, and community mistrust. Rapid tests could help, but none are approved for Bundibugyo yet; development could take months.

article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Ministry of Health remains on alert for severe cases of respiratory syndromes, according to Fiocruz.
article.articleSummary: As of 11 June 2026, Brazil faces ongoing SRAG (Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome) activity, with Mato Grosso do Sul reporting elevated incidence per Fiocruz InfoGripe and Campo Grande among nine capitals with high SRAG activity, though not showing a sustained recent rise. Central-West hospitalizations remain high for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), a leading cause of hospitalization in young children. Influenza B cases are rising in Mato Grosso do Sul, São Paulo and Paraná. Nationally, SRAG increases are driven mainly by RSV in children up to 4 years; rhinovirus predominates in ages 5–14; influenza A accounts for most severe cases in older youth, adults, and seniors. Preventive measures include frequent hand hygiene, masking in health settings and crowded indoors, isolation when symptomatic, and vaccination against influenza and RSV for priority groups. By 2026 there have been 82,500 SRAG cases and 3,591 deaths nationwide, with RSV, influenza A, and rhinovirus most identified.

article.articleSummary: Outbreak of Bundibugyo ebolavirus in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda is driving accelerated vaccine development. These efforts aim to deliver safe, effective vaccines and strengthen outbreak preparedness and response against this rising epidemic.

article.articleSummary: Redwood AI Corp. signs a non-binding Letter of Intent with Dr. Placide Sesonga of the University of Global Health Equity (Rwanda) to develop a regional pathogen-tracking and AI-enabled outbreak intelligence initiative across Central and East Africa, focusing on Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). The LOI supports protocol development, an operational deployment framework, and prioritization of surveillance sites, with engagement of the Rwandan Ministry of Health and regional partners; any binding commitments would require definitive agreements.

With Amazonian summer approaching, authorities emphasize community participation to eliminate breeding sites and sustain vigilance.

article.articleSummary: Shigellosis is a highly contagious bacterial diarrhoeal disease caused by Shigella, transmitted via the faecal-oral route and spread by five 'F's (food, faeces, fingers, flies, fomites). In Kerala, past outbreaks include about 40 cases in Kozhikode in 2020; Shigella is present in Kerala, Maharashtra and Assam, mainly affecting children under five and the elderly. Nipah is a zoonotic virus that causes respiratory illness and acute encephalitis; transmission from fruit bats and via contaminated raw date palm sap or contact with infected animals. Nipah emerged in Kozhikode in 2018, with 17 of 18 infected dying; Kerala has since seen about two-dozen Nipah deaths. Mortality for Nipah ranges 40-75%. Prevention includes hygiene, clean water, latrine use, avoiding bats, and PPE; treatment: Shigella hydration and supportive care; Nipah lacks specific therapy, but early diagnosis with high-quality supportive care improves outcomes. Seasonal outbreaks accompany Kerala’s early monsoon.

article.articleSummary: As of 12 June 2026, laboratory tests detected bacterial contamination in wastewater and drinking water near Kent Mahal Apartments in Brahmapuram, Kochi. The long-running sewage and solid waste dispute, raised about nine years ago by Vadavucode-Puthencruz residents, involves wastewater discharge from the Kent Mahal complex affecting nearby water bodies, fields and homes. The Community Health Centre, Vadavucode, sent two channel-discharge water samples to the Regional Public Health Laboratory, which found coliform bacteria. Drinking water samples from nearby wells were analyzed at the Regional Analytical Laboratory, Kakkanad, showing both coliform bacteria and E. coli, signaling groundwater quality concerns in the area. The results renew attention on the unresolved controversy, which has included official interventions and court proceedings without resolution.

article.articleHeadline: Recurring Nipah outbreaks in Kerala linked to ecological changes, says recent study
article.articleSummary: Recurring Nipah outbreaks in Kerala are linked to ecological changes, habitat disruption, and increasing human–wildlife interaction, according to a May 13 study 'Two geographies, one virus: What recurrent Nipah spillover in India reveals' by Deepak Y Patil, Rima R Sahay, Sreelekshmy Mohandas and Pragya D Yadav. The researchers note deforestation and loss of natural habitats in biodiversity-rich regions may raise opportunities for viruses to cross from animals to humans. In Kerala, Nipah outbreaks have historically occurred between April and September, when hot, humid conditions and seasonal fruits attract fruit bats (Pteropus spp.) closer to settlements, creating direct or indirect contact with humans and domestic animals. Nipah virus (NiV) is primarily maintained in fruit bats and is a highly infectious pathogen capable of causing severe illness in humans. Kerala's strong disease surveillance and rapid public health response have helped prevent larger outbreaks, underscoring ecology as a driver of recurrent spillovers.

article.articleHeadline: Ebola is back. So are the double standards
article.articleSummary: Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo began May 15, with 617 confirmed cases and 117 deaths by June 9. It has spread to Uganda; officials fear it could eclipse the West Africa death toll. Bundibugyo, with no approved vaccine or specific treatment, relies on supportive care. Transmission is via contact with bodily fluids, not airborne; control hinges on contact tracing and infection control, challenged by distrust and burial practices. The first confirmed case was a Bunia healthcare worker on April 25; origin likely animal spillover before human transmission. Globally, the US plans an Ebola quarantine facility in Kenya for Americans working in or traveling through outbreak areas, while Kenya's Laikipia Air Base quarantine centre was ordered closed; travel bans by US/Canada hinder response, drawing critique from WHO and health leaders. Past Bundibugyo outbreaks were smaller: Uganda 2007 (131 cases) and DRC 2012 (38).

article.articleHeadline: Ebola-Ausbruch: Virus trifft belastete Region - Deutsches Ärzteblatt
article.articleHeadlineTranslated: Ebola Outbreak: Virus Hits Hard-Hit Region
article.articleSummary: An outbreak of Bundibugyo ebolavirus (BDBV) is challenging North-East Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) and neighboring Uganda, with late May 2026 lab confirmation in several regions. Eight of the first 13 samples tested positive, indicating a broader, under-recognized spread. BDBV is rarer, lacks rapid diagnostics or approved vaccines or antivirals, and standard Ebola PCR tests may fail. The first known case was a caregiver who fell ill on 24 April and died on 27 April in Bunia, Ituri province, suggesting wider transmission before detection. Genomic sequencing in mid-May showed substantial differences from prior outbreaks, pointing to spillover from an animal reservoir rather than sustained endemic circulation. Symptoms begin flu-like, then progress to rash, chest pain, and hemorrhagic signs; mortality appears not as high as other species. Kontrol relies on isolation, contact tracing, quarantine, and local lab capacity; trials are underway for Remdesivir and MBP134, with Maftivimab also considered. A post-exposure prophylaxis approach is also being explored by WHO.
